<reason>The decisive clash was whether PRO's "sequencing" rule actually reduces the certain cost (interest) it invoked as its trigger. PRO's own concession that its policy is "a pause on addition, not a program of subtraction," combined with its admission of no ten-year savings figure, let CON build a devastating and sustained line: since interest is driven by existing stock, rates, and legacy programs rather than new commitments, PRO's rule spends real, datable investment value to buy zero reduction in the very number PRO's opening leaned on. CON hammered this from Rebuttal 2 through Closing, and PRO's Closing pivoted to a "who bears the risk of being wrong" frame without directly refuting that the rule produces no risk reduction at all — leaving CON's strongest point effectively unanswered. PRO did land some good counters (the tax-cut symmetry argument, distinguishing the Eurozone austerity comparison, and pressing CON for its own threshold), and CON never gave a fully precise threshold either, but CON's conceptual trigger (interest crowding out current obligations) plus its CBO/PAYGO mechanism answered the pressure questions more substantively than PRO's admitted absence of a savings figure. CON's opening being clipped is a real execution cost, but the surviving material still carried the decisive argument through to the end.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's exploitation of PRO's own concession ("a pause on addition, not a program of subtraction," no ten-year savings figure) in Rebuttal 2 and Closing — showing PRO's rule buys zero reduction in the certain cost it built its whole case on — was the single most damaging and unanswered blow in the debate.</best_rebuttal>
